title: Welcome to Cold War Two: historian Niall Ferguson on geopolitics in 2026
summary: Historian Niall Ferguson at Davos 2026 on a US-China Cold War II made riskier by AI, polarization that falls short of civil war, and why today's dangers are small by historical standards.

assertions.quote: this looks quite like a cold war now between the United States and China, two superpowers.

verdicts.note: A common and useful analogy for the rivalry since about 2018, but the two economies are far more entwined than the US and Soviet ones were.
DDIS describes a long-term strategic rivalry with competing blocs of partners, arms and AI competition, but does not call it a cold war and expects turbulence rather than a fixed standoff.
Eurasia Group's 2026 outlook says there is not (yet) a second Cold War, with China remaking the global system and the US and allies resisting.

assertions.quote: artificial intelligence is probably the most important that make this Cold War in some ways a more dangerous and unpredictable one than the first one.

verdicts.note: A judgment about an unfolding technology with no settled evidence.

RAND workshop experts agreed advanced AI could severely compromise strategic stability and that the resulting strategic arrangements could prove less stable than those of the US-Soviet Cold War, a forecast to 2040 rather than a finding about the US-China rivalry today.

assertions.quote: By comparison with I don't know the world in 1926 or 36 or 46. The geopolitical problems of 2026 are really quite minor.

verdicts.note: No great-power war is under way and war deaths are far below those decades, but nuclear arsenals and arms control are in flux and the Doomsday Clock is at its closest.
OWID: three-quarters of combatant war deaths since 1800 came in the two World Wars, and recent decades saw fewer conflict deaths than most of the 20th century, but deaths are rising again.

The WEF report says conflict-risk indicators are at their worst since the Second World War. That fits today being calmer than the 1940s, but it contradicts the claim that today's dangers are small next to the worst of the Cold War.

assertions.quote: there's an arms race going on in the Indo-Pacific region.

verdicts.note: China's naval, missile and nuclear build-up and the US and allied responses meet common definitions of an arms race.
DDIS: the US and China compete to develop advanced weapons, China is intensifying its build-up (the US less so), and the Pacific balance is shifting toward China.

assertions.quote: That's the kind of competition that historically has produced war.

verdicts.note: Studies find arms races raise the odds that disputes escalate, but many ended without war, the Cold War among them.

In the case file, Germany's naval build-up set off a fierce arms race with Britain that helped bring the First World War. The same file's Cold War case (L364) is an arms race that ended without war, so arms races sometimes preceded war rather than always leading to it.

assertions.quote: I'm very wary of the idea of cycles because I I don't think there are cycles in history.

verdicts.note: A position in the philosophy of history.
Clauset: interstate war onsets since 1823 fit a simple Poisson process with a constant hazard, meaning random, memoryless timing rather than cycles (for interstate war only).

Hanania concludes that history may be of limited use for understanding US-China relations and that no one has shown that conclusions drawn from the distant past survive basic scrutiny. Allison himself concedes he proposes no 'iron laws' (L159-165).

assertions.quote: that makes it quite hard to sustain narratives of extraordinary polarization tending towards civil war. I actually think that's highly unlikely

verdicts.note: Polarization is real but geographically mixed and political violence remains far below civil-war levels.

assertions.quote: It's extraordinarily nasty this war because the weapons are are really thanks to drone technology very lethal

verdicts.note: Ukrainian and Western estimates attribute most battlefield casualties on both sides to drones.
EFIS cites Ukraine's commander-in-chief that drones cause up to 70% of losses of weapons and equipment, which shows drones dominate attrition but not whether the war is unusually deadly overall.
